source_text: Πᾶσα γὰρ ἡ δόξα τῆς θυγατρὸς τοῦ βασιλέως, φησὶν, ἔσωθεν. Ἐὰν ἔχῃς προαίρεσιν φιλόξενον, ἅπασαν τῆς φιλοξενίας ἔχεις τὴν θήκην, κἂν ὀβολὸν ᾖς κεκτημένος μόνον· ἂν δὲ μισάνθρωπος ᾖς καὶ μισόξενος, κἂν τὰ πάντα ᾖς περιβεβλημένος πράγματα, ἐστενοχώρηταί σοι τοῖς ξένοις ἡ οἰκία. Οὐκ εἶχεν αὕτη κλίνας ἀργυρενδέτους, ἀλλ' εἶχε σωφροσύνην πολλήν· οὐκ εἶχε στρωμνὴν, ἀλλὰ προαίρεσιν ἐκέκτητο προσηνῆ καὶ φιλόξενον· οὐκ εἶχε κίονας ἀπαστράπτοντας, ἀλλ' εἶχε ψυχῆς κάλλος ἀπολάμπον· οὐκ εἶχε τοίχους μαρμάροις περιβεβλημένους, οὐδὲ ἔδαφος ψηφῖσι διηνθισμένον, ἀλλ' ἦν αὐτὴ ναὸς τοῦ Πνεύματος. Ταῦτα ἐπῄνεσεν ὁ Παῦλος, τούτων ἠράσθη· διὰ ταῦτα ἔτη δύο μείνας ἐπὶ τῆς οἰκίας οὐκ ἀπανίστατο· διὰ ταῦτα αὐτῶν μέμνηται διηνεκῶς, καὶ ἐγκώμιον αὐτοῖς συντίθησι μέγα καὶ θαυμαστὸν, οὐχ ἵνα αὐτοὺς λαμπροτέρους ἐργάσηται, ἀλλ' ἵνα τοὺς λοιποὺς εἰς τὸν αὐτὸν ἀγάγῃ ζῆλον, καὶ πείσῃ μακαρίζειν, οὐχὶ τοὺς πλουτοῦντας, οὐδὲ τοὺς ἐν ἀρχαῖς ὄντας, ἀλλὰ τοὺς φιλοξένους, τοὺς ἐλεήμονας, τοὺς φιλανθρώπους, τοὺς πολλὴν περὶ τοὺς ἁγίους φιλοφροσύνην ἐπιδεικνυμένους. εʹ. Ταῦτα δὴ καὶ ἡμεῖς ἀπὸ τῆς προσρήσεως ταύτης μαθόντες, διὰ τῶν ἔργων αὐτῶν ἐπιδειξώμεθα· καὶ μήτε τοὺς πλουτοῦντας ἁπλῶς μακαρίζωμεν, μήτε τοὺς πτωχοὺς ἐξευτελίζωμεν, μηδὲ ἐπαισχυνώμεθα τέχναις, μηδὲ ὄνειδος εἶναι νομίζωμεν ἐργασίαν, ἀλλὰ ἀργίαν, καὶ τὸ μὴ ἔχειν τι ποιεῖν. Εἰ γὰρ ὄνειδος ἦν τὸ ἐργάζεσθαι, οὐκ ἂν αὐτὸ μετῆλθεν ὁ Παῦλος, οὐκ ἂν ἐπ' αὐτῷ μεῖζον ἐφρόνησεν, οὕτω λέγων· Ἐὰν γὰρ εὐαγγελίζωμαι, οὐκ ἔστι μοι καύχημα. Τίς οὖν μοί ἐστιν ὁ μισθός; Ἵνα εὐαγγελιζόμενος ἀδάπανον θήσω τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον τοῦ Χριστοῦ. Εἰ δὲ τέχνη ὄνειδος ἦν, οὐκ ἂν τοὺς μὴ ἐργαζομένους ἐκέλευσε μηδὲ ἐσθίειν. Ἁμαρτία γὰρ μόνον ἐστὶν ὄνειδος· ταύτην δὲ ἀργία τίκτειν εἴωθε, καὶ οὐ μίαν καὶ δύο καὶ τρεῖς μόνον, ἀλλὰ πᾶσαν ὁμοῦ τὴν πονηρίαν. Διὰ τοῦτο καί τις σοφὸς δεικνὺς, ὅτι πᾶσαν τὴν κακίαν ἐδίδαξεν ἡ ἀργία, καὶ περὶ οἰκετῶν διαλεγόμενός φησιν· Ἔμβαλε αὐτὸν εἰς ἔργον, ἵνα μὴ ἀργῇ. Ὅπερ γάρ ἐστιν ὁ χαλινὸς τῷ ἵππῳ, τοῦτο τὸ ἔργον τῇ φύσει τῇ ἡμετέρᾳ. Εἰ καλὸν ἦν ἡ ἀργία, πάντα ἂν ἄσπαρτα καὶ ἀνήροτα ἡ γῆ ἀνεβλάστανεν· ἀλλ' οὐδὲν τοιοῦτον ἐργάζεται. Πρώην μὲν οὖν ἐκέλευσεν ἀνήροτα πάντα ἐκβαλεῖν ὁ Θεός· νυνὶ δὲ οὐκ ἐποίησεν οὕτως, ἀλλὰ καὶ ζεῦξαι βόας, καὶ ἄροτρον ἑλκύσαι, καὶ αὔλακα ἀνατεμεῖν, καὶ σπέρματα καταβάλλειν, καὶ ἑτέροις πολλοῖς τρόποις θεραπεῦσαι καὶ ἄμπελον καὶ δένδρα καὶ σπέρματα τοῖς ἀνθρώποις ἐνομοθέτησεν, ἵν' ἡ τῆς ἐργασίας ἀσχολία πάσης ἀπάγῃ πονηρίας τὴν τῶν ἐργαζομένων διάνοιαν. Ἐξ ἀρχῆς μὲν οὖν, ἵνα τὴν δύναμιν ἐπιδείξηται τὴν ἑαυτοῦ, χωρὶς τῶν πόνων τῶν ἡμετέρων ἅπαντα ἀναδοθῆναι παρεσκεύασε· Βλαστησάτω γὰρ ἡ γῆ βοτάνην χόρτου, φησί· καὶ πάντα ἐκόμα εὐθέως· μετὰ δὲ ταῦτα οὐχ οὕτως· ἀλλὰ καὶ διὰ τῶν ἡμετέρων αὐτὰ πόνων ἐκφέρεσθαι ἐκέλευσεν ἐκ τῆς γῆς, ἵνα μάθῃς ὅτι διὰ τὸ χρήσιμον ἡμῖν καὶ λυσιτελὲς τὸν πόνον εἰσήγαγε. Καὶ δοκεῖ μὲν εἶναι κόλασις καὶ τιμωρία τὸ ἀκοῦσαι, Ἐν ἱδρῶτι τοῦ προσώπου σου φάγῃ τὸν ἄρτον σου· τὸ δὲ ἀληθὲς, νουθεσία τίς ἐστι καὶ σωφρονισμὸς, καὶ τῶν τραυμάτων τῶν ἀπὸ τῆς ἁμαρτίας γενομένων φάρμακον.
thought_title: True adornment is within; work is no disgrace
orientation: Chrysostom is still expounding Paul's greeting to Priscilla and Aquila, now contrasting outward wealth with inner virtue and defending manual labor against the charge of shame.
pass_a_gloss: For all the glory of the daughter of the king, he says, is from within. If you have a hospitable disposition, you have the whole treasury of hospitality, even if you possess only an obol; but if you are a hater of people and a hater of strangers, even if you are clothed with all things, your house is cramped for strangers. She did not have silver-bound couches, but she had much self-control; she did not have bedding, but she had acquired a gentle and hospitable disposition; she did not have flashing pillars, but she had beauty of soul shining forth; she did not have walls clothed with marbles, nor a floor embroidered with mosaic stones, but she herself was a temple of the Spirit. These things Paul praised, these things he loved; because of these things, staying two years at the house, he did not depart; because of these things he remembers them continually, and he composes for them a great and wondrous encomium, not in order to make them more illustrious, but in order to lead the rest to the same zeal, and to persuade them to call blessed, not the rich, nor those in positions of power, but the hospitable, the merciful, the lovers of people, those displaying much kindness toward the saints. 5. Having learned these things then from this greeting, let us display them through our own deeds; and let us neither simply call the rich blessed, nor despise the poor, nor be ashamed of crafts, nor consider work a reproach, but idleness, and the having nothing to do. For if working were a reproach, Paul would not have pursued it, he would not have taken greater pride in it, saying thus: For if I preach the gospel, there is no boast for me. What then is my reward? That preaching the gospel I may set forth the gospel of Christ without cost. But if a craft were a reproach, he would not have commanded those who do not work not even to eat. For sin alone is a reproach; and idleness is accustomed to give birth to this, and not one and two and three only, but all wickedness together. Therefore also a certain wise man, showing that idleness taught all evil, also speaking about household servants says: Put him to work, so that he may not be idle. For what the bridle is to the horse, this work is to our nature. If idleness were good, the earth would have brought forth all things unsown and unplowed; but it produces no such thing. Formerly then God commanded all things to come forth unplowed; but now he did not do thus, but also to yoke oxen, and to drag the plow, and to cut the furrow, and to cast down seeds, and to tend in many other ways both vine and trees and seeds he legislated for humans, in order that the occupation of work may lead away the mind of those who work from all wickedness. From the beginning then, in order to display his own power, he prepared all things to be produced without our labors; For let the earth sprout the herb of grass, he says; and all things flourished immediately; but after these things not thus; but he commanded them to be brought forth from the earth also through our labors, in order that you may learn that for our benefit and advantage he introduced labor. And it seems to be a punishment and penalty to hear, In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread; but the truth is, it is a certain admonition and correction, and a medicine for the wounds that came from sin.

choices.why: θήκη means a chest or storehouse; 'treasury' captures the sense of a full store of hospitality's riches, matching the contrast with possessing only an obol.
The compound is transparently 'people-hater'; rendering it as a phrase preserves the parallel with μισόξενος ('hater of strangers') and avoids a single abstract English word.

choices.term: ἐστενοχώρηταί σοι τοῖς ξένοις ἡ οἰκία
choices.english: your house is cramped for strangers
choices.why: The dative τοῖς ξένοις is a dative of reference; 'cramped for strangers' keeps the literal sense that the house has no room for them, despite the owner's wealth.
rejected: your house is too narrow for strangers
your house has no room for strangers

choices.why: Literal rendering of ναός as 'temple' and the genitive as possessive; she herself was a dwelling place of the Holy Spirit, contrasting with the marble walls she lacked.

choices.english: I may set forth the gospel of Christ without cost
choices.why: ἀδάπανον means 'without expense'; 'set forth without cost' preserves the literal sense of presenting the gospel at no charge to the hearers.
rejected: I may make the gospel free of charge
I may present the gospel without expense

choices.why: The imperative ἔμβαλε with εἰς ἔργον is a direct command; 'put him to work' is the plain literal rendering, matching the context of household servants.

pass_b_english: For all the glory of the king's daughter is within, he says (Psalm 45:13 LXX). If you have a hospitable disposition, you possess the entire treasury of hospitality, even if you own only a single obol. But if you are a hater of people and a hater of strangers, even if you are wrapped in every kind of wealth, your house is cramped for strangers. She did not have couches inlaid with silver, but she had abundant self-control. She did not have fine bedding, but she possessed a gentle and hospitable disposition. She did not have flashing columns, but she had a beauty of soul that shone forth. She did not have walls covered in marble or a floor adorned with mosaic stones, but she herself was a temple of the Spirit. These are the things Paul praised; these are the things he loved. For these reasons he stayed in her house for two years and would not leave. For these reasons he remembers them constantly and composes for them a great and wondrous encomium—not to make them more illustrious, but to lead everyone else to the same zeal and to persuade them to call blessed not the rich, nor those in positions of power, but the hospitable, the merciful, the lovers of humanity, those who show great kindness toward the saints.

Since we have learned these things from this greeting, let us demonstrate them through our own deeds. Let us not simply call the rich blessed, nor despise the poor. Let us not be ashamed of trades, nor consider work a disgrace—but rather idleness, and having nothing to do. For if working were a disgrace, Paul would not have pursued it, nor would he have taken pride in it, saying: For if I preach the gospel, I have no ground for boasting (1 Corinthians 9:16). What then is my reward? That when I preach, I may set forth the gospel of Christ without cost (1 Corinthians 9:18). And if a trade were a disgrace, he would not have commanded those who do not work not to eat (2 Thessalonians 3:10). For sin alone is a disgrace, and idleness is accustomed to give birth to it—not just one or two or three sins, but every kind of wickedness all at once. That is why a certain wise man, showing that idleness has taught all evil, says when speaking about household servants: Put him to work, so that he may not be idle (Sirach 33:28). For what the bridle is to the horse, work is to our nature. If idleness were good, the earth would produce everything unsown and unplowed. But it does nothing of the sort. In the beginning, God commanded the earth to bring forth everything unplowed; but now he has not done it that way. Instead, he has given laws to human beings to yoke oxen, to drag the plow, to cut the furrow, to cast down seeds, and to tend the vine and the trees and the seeds in many other ways, so that the occupation of work may draw the minds of those who labor away from every wickedness. From the beginning, then, to display his own power, he arranged for all things to spring up without our labors. Let the earth sprout forth the herb of grass, he says (Genesis 1:11), and immediately everything flourished. But after that, not so. Instead, he commanded that these things be brought forth from the earth through our own labors, so that you might learn that he introduced toil for our benefit and advantage. And hearing, In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread (Genesis 3:19), seems to be a punishment and a penalty, but in truth it is an admonition and a discipline, and a medicine for the wounds that came from sin.

last_rejected.why: The command is from Paul (2 Thess 3:10), but Greek says 'he would not have commanded'; subject is Paul from prior clause, not Christ.
last_rejected.fix: he would not have commanded those not working not to eat
last_rejected.ruling: Subject is Paul from context; 'he' correctly refers back, no misleading reference.

last_rejected.quote: Put him to work, so that he may not be idle

last_rejected.why: ἀργῇ is subjunctive 'he may be idle,' but context demands 'so that he may not be idle'—correct in meaning but check if 'put him to work' captures ἔμβαλε forcefully enough.
last_rejected.fix: Throw him into work, so that he not be idle
last_rejected.ruling: Translation is correct; ἔμβαλε as 'put to work' captures the force adequately.

last_rejected.why: ἀσχολία means preoccupation/busyness, not occupation; 'occupation of work' is tautological and misses sense.
last_rejected.ruling: ἀσχολία as occupation/busyness is within range; not a major error.

last_rejected.ruling: εἰσήγαγε means 'introduced'; within normal range, not a major error.
